questions.primaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt:
Researchers recruit 90 adult volunteers from one community who report that they frequently experience nausea in virtual-reality environments. The researchers want to study whether an active acupressure wristband helps users complete a standardized 20-minute virtual-reality ride without ending early because of nausea.

Each volunteer receives either an active wristband or a visually identical sham wristband. The wristbands are supplied in coded packages. The participants and the evaluator who records whether each ride is completed do not know which type was used. Results are shown.

Treatment          Completed ride   Ended early   Total
Active wristband         34              11         45
Sham wristband           24              21         45

(a) Identify the population of interest, the sample, and the experimental units.

(b) Identify the treatments and response variable. State a statistical question the experiment is designed to answer.

(c) Describe a valid random-assignment procedure for placing the 90 volunteers into two groups of 45. Explain the purpose of random assignment.

(d) Explain the purposes of the sham wristband and the blinding used in the experiment.

(e) Calculate and interpret the observed difference in completion proportions, active minus sham. State the causal and generalization conclusions that this design could support if the difference is judged meaningful.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies the population of interest as adults who frequently experience nausea in virtual-reality environments and the sample as the 90 recruited volunteers from the community.
· Point 2: Identifies the 90 individual volunteers as the experimental units.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies the active and sham wristbands as the treatments and ride completion without ending early because of nausea as the binary response variable.
· Point 2: States a comparative statistical question about whether the probability or proportion completing the ride differs between active- and sham-wristband conditions.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Describes a valid chance process, such as randomly shuffling all 90 participant labels and assigning the first 45 to active and the remaining 45 to sham.
· Point 2: Explains that random assignment tends to balance preexisting characteristics and other potential confounders between groups, supporting a cause-and-effect comparison.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that the visually identical sham controls for placebo effects and for the experience of wearing a wristband.
· Point 2: Explains that blinding participants limits response or expectation effects and blinding the evaluator limits differential outcome assessment.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates p̂active − p̂sham = 34/45 − 24/45 = 10/45 ≈ 0.222 and interprets it as a completion rate about 22.2 percentage points higher in the active group.
· Point 2: States that random assignment can support a causal conclusion for volunteers like those studied, but volunteer recruitment does not support generalization to all adults who experience virtual-reality nausea.
questions.modelResponse:
The volunteers are both the sampled people and the experimental units, while the broader target is adults prone to virtual-reality nausea. Randomly assign participant labels to two equal groups before distributing coded bands. This creates treatment groups that should be similar on average with respect to susceptibility, prior experience, and other background variables.

The sham band gives both groups the same visible treatment experience, and the two forms of blinding reduce expectation and evaluator effects. The observed completion proportions are 34/45 ≈ 0.756 and 24/45 ≈ 0.533, a difference of about 0.222. The experiment can attribute a meaningful difference to the active band among the volunteers because treatment was randomized. Since the participants volunteered rather than being randomly sampled from the target population, broader generalization requires caution.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A sports-science center records choice-reaction times for two standardized goalkeeper drills. Reaction times for athletes in the center's reference population are each adequately modeled by a normal distribution. Lower times indicate faster reactions.

Drill                    Mean   Standard deviation   One goalkeeper's time
Visual-choice drill     480 ms         40 ms                420 ms
Auditory-choice drill   360 ms         30 ms                318 ms

(a) Calculate the goalkeeper's z-score for each drill. Determine in which drill the goalkeeper performed better relative to the corresponding reference distribution.

(b) Calculate the percentile of the goalkeeper's reaction time in each drill. Interpret the visual-choice percentile in context, accounting for the fact that lower times are better.

(c) For a randomly selected athlete from the visual-choice reference population, calculate the probability of a reaction time between 440 ms and 520 ms. Interpret the result.

(d) The center defines the fastest 5% on the visual-choice drill as elite. The z-score with 0.05 area to its left is −1.645. Determine the reaction-time cutoff for elite status and whether the goalkeeper qualifies.

(e) Suppose a later histogram of visual-choice times is strongly right-skewed because a few athletes have very slow responses. Explain how that finding would affect the normal-model calculations in parts (b) through (d).
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates zvisual = (420 − 480)/40 = −1.50 and zauditory = (318 − 360)/30 = −1.40.
· Point 2: Concludes that the visual-choice performance is better relative to its reference group because −1.50 represents a reaction time farther below the mean and lower times are better.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates P(Z ≤ −1.50) ≈ 0.0668 and P(Z ≤ −1.40) ≈ 0.0808, placing the times at about the 6.7th and 8.1st percentiles, respectively.
· Point 2: Interprets the visual result: about 6.7% of reference athletes have times at or below 420 ms, so this goalkeeper is faster than about 93.3% of that reference population.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Standardizes 440 ms and 520 ms as z = −1 and z = 1 and calculates P(−1 ≤ Z ≤ 1) ≈ 0.6827.
· Point 2: Interprets the result: about 68.3% of athletes in the visual-choice reference population are expected to have reaction times from 440 ms through 520 ms.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates the cutoff as x = 480 + (−1.645)(40) = 414.2 ms.
· Point 2: Concludes that elite status requires a time at or below about 414.2 ms, so the goalkeeper's 420 ms does not qualify.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that strong right skew conflicts with the stated normal model, especially for percentile and tail calculations.
· Point 2: States that the numerical probabilities and 5% cutoff could then be inaccurate and that the center should use the empirical distribution or another suitable model instead.
questions.modelResponse:
Standardization allows comparison across drills with different means and standard deviations. The goalkeeper is 1.50 standard deviations faster than the visual mean and 1.40 standard deviations faster than the auditory mean, so the visual result is relatively stronger. Normal-table areas to the left are approximately 0.0668 and 0.0808. Because short times are desirable, a low percentile corresponds to strong performance.

For the visual drill, 440 ms and 520 ms are one standard deviation below and above the mean, giving a central probability near 0.6827. The fastest 5% lie below 480 − 1.645(40) = 414.2 ms; 420 ms is not fast enough for that cutoff. These results depend on a credible normal model. Strong right skew would make normal tail areas and a normal-based elite cutoff questionable.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A meal-delivery company buys insulated lunch containers from two suppliers. For each supplier, a quality analyst takes an independent simple random sample from that supplier's current production. The response is the number of hours a sealed container keeps its contents above a specified food-safe temperature in a standardized laboratory test.

Supplier   Sample size, n   Sample mean, x̄   Sample standard deviation, s
A                22              9.84 hours              0.62 hour
B                20              9.31 hours              0.71 hour

Side-by-side dotplots for the two samples are roughly symmetric with no apparent outliers. Each supplier produced more than 220 containers during the sampling period. For a 90% confidence interval using the conservative degrees of freedom df = 38, use t* = 1.686.

(a) Define the population parameter to be estimated and identify the appropriate confidence-interval procedure.

(b) Check the conditions for the confidence-interval procedure.

(c) Calculate the standard error and margin of error, and construct a 90% confidence interval for μA − μB.

(d) Interpret the confidence interval in context.

(e) A purchasing manager claims that Supplier A's containers have a mean safe-temperature duration at least 0.25 hour longer than Supplier B's. Use the interval to evaluate the claim.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Defines μA − μB as the difference between the true mean safe-temperature durations for the current production of containers from Suppliers A and B.
· Point 2: Selects an independent two-sample t confidence interval for a difference in population means.
(b) 3 points
· Point 1: Cites the two independent simple random samples and the independence of the supplier groups.
· Point 2: Verifies the 10% condition because 22 and 20 are no more than 10% of the corresponding suppliers' production totals.
· Point 3: Uses the roughly symmetric, outlier-free dotplots to justify t procedures for the two relatively small samples.
(c) 3 points
· Point 1: Calculates SE = √[(0.62²/22) + (0.71²/20)] ≈ 0.2066 hour.
· Point 2: Calculates the margin of error as 1.686(0.2066) ≈ 0.3483 hour.
· Point 3: Constructs (9.84 − 9.31) ± 0.3483, giving the interval (0.182, 0.878) hour, allowing for minor rounding differences.
(d) 1 point
· Point 1: States that the analyst is 90% confident that Supplier A's current-production containers have a true mean safe-temperature duration between about 0.182 and 0.878 hour longer than Supplier B's.
(e) 1 point
· Point 1: States that the interval supports a positive mean advantage for Supplier A but does not support an advantage of at least 0.25 hour because plausible differences from approximately 0.182 to 0.25 are included.
questions.modelResponse:
The samples come independently from two production populations, and the response is quantitative with unknown population standard deviations. Therefore, use a two-sample t interval for μA − μB. Random sampling, the 10% checks, and the roughly symmetric sample distributions without outliers support the method.

The observed difference is 0.53 hour. Its estimated standard error is about 0.2066, and multiplication by t* = 1.686 gives a margin of error near 0.3483. The 90% interval is approximately (0.182, 0.878) hour. All values are positive, so Supplier A likely has the larger population mean for current production. However, the interval contains positive differences smaller than 0.25 hour, so it does not establish the manager's stronger minimum-advantage claim.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
A small theater has five stage backdrops. The hours required to repaint the five backdrops during the previous season were

6, 8, 10, 13, 18.

The theater manager will select a simple random sample of 2 different backdrops, without replacement, and use the sample mean x̄ to estimate the mean repainting time for all 5 backdrops. There are C(5, 2) = 10 equally likely unordered samples.

(a) Calculate the population mean and median repainting times. Compare the two measures of center in light of the data pattern.

(b) List all 10 possible samples of 2 backdrops and calculate x̄ for each. Construct the probability distribution of x̄.

(c) On paper, sketch a dotplot of the sampling distribution of x̄. Label the axis, and state the center and range of the sampling distribution.

(d) Calculate the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄. Explain what the result shows about x̄ as an estimator of the population mean.

(e) Calculate the probability that x̄ is within 2 hours, inclusive, of the population mean. Use the probability to evaluate the manager's claim that an SRS of 2 has at least a 75% chance of estimating the population mean within 2 hours.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates the population mean μ = (6 + 8 + 10 + 13 + 18)/5 = 11 hours and the median as 10 hours.
· Point 2: Explains that the high value 18 pulls the mean above the median, consistent with a distribution having a longer upper side.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Lists the 10 samples and means correctly: (6, 8) → 7; (6, 10) → 8; (6, 13) → 9.5; (6, 18) → 12; (8, 10) → 9; (8, 13) → 10.5; (8, 18) → 13; (10, 13) → 11.5; (10, 18) → 14; (13, 18) → 15.5.
· Point 2: Gives the sampling distribution with x̄ values 7, 8, 9, 9.5, 10.5, 11.5, 12, 13, 14, and 15.5, each having probability 0.10.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Draws one dot at each of the 10 possible x̄ values on a horizontal axis labeled “sample mean repainting time, x̄ (hours).”
· Point 2: States that the sampling distribution is centered at 11 hours and ranges from 7 to 15.5 hours, for a range of 8.5 hours.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates μx̄ = [7 + 8 + 9 + 9.5 + 10.5 + 11.5 + 12 + 13 + 14 + 15.5]/10 = 11 hours.
· Point 2: Explains that the sampling-distribution mean equals the population mean, showing that x̄ is an unbiased estimator of μ under this SRS process.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies 6 qualifying means from 9 through 13 inclusive and calculates P(|x̄ − 11| ≤ 2) = 6/10 = 0.60.
· Point 2: Rejects the manager's claim because 0.60 is less than 0.75; the exact sampling distribution gives only a 60% chance of being within 2 hours.
questions.modelResponse:
The population mean is 11 hours and the median is 10 hours. The 18-hour backdrop raises the mean above the median. For an SRS of two, enumerate unordered pairs rather than ordered selections; each of the 10 pairs has probability 0.10. Their means are 7, 8, 9, 9.5, 10.5, 11.5, 12, 13, 14, and 15.5, so the dotplot contains one point at each value.

Averaging those 10 sample means gives 11 hours, exactly the population mean. This establishes unbiasedness for the stated sampling process, but unbiasedness does not guarantee that every individual estimate is close. Only the six means from 9 through 13 lie within 2 hours of 11, producing probability 0.60 and contradicting the claimed 75% success rate.
